text.p: Israel's Leumi Insurance Holdings said on Tuesday that the insurance commissioner had approved Assicurazioni Generali's planned takeover of the company.

But Michael Kleiner, the lawmaker who heads the parliamentary finance sub-committee on insurance, promised to continue his battle to force Generali to compensate the families of policy-holders who perished in the Holocaust.

The approval clears the way for Generali to make a tender offer to Leumi Insurance shareholders. The Italian insurer faces accusations that it has failed to honour life insurance policies taken out before the Second World War by victims of the Holocaust.
A Treasury spokesman, confirming the decision, said the issue of compensation was not in the purview of the insurance commissioner.

A source close to the parliamentary committee said he expected a stormy session when the panel meets on Wednesday and that some legislators might urge Israelis to boycott Migdal, Leumi Insurance's main insurance subsidiary.
"Under the agreement, Generali will be allowed to hold 60 percent of Migdal and (and a second subsidiary) Sela," Leumi Insurance said in a statement to the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange on Tuesday.

"Bank Leumi will be allowed to hold 25 percent of those companies. Bank Leumi will be allowed to reduce its holdings and Generali will be allowed to increase its holdings by five percent. Generali will be able to sell or transfer part of its holdings on condition it retain at least 33 percent of the holdings," the statement said.
Bank Leumi, which arranged the Generali takeover, is under legislative mandate to reduce its holdings in non-bank companies like Leumi Insurance Holdings to 25 percent and later to 20 percent.

Generali is due to make a $300 million tender offer to shareholders in Leumi Insurance that will leave the Italian company with 57 percent holding. The offer is expected to be made sometime this month.
The offer was supposed to have been made in February but has been held up by government approvals, which officials said were not connected with the Holocaust-related claims.
A spokesman for Generali would not comment on the announcement.
